title: Alliances with Foreign Powers
lead: May God's people make treaties with foreign empires? The prophets warned Judah's kings against trusting Egypt or Assyria instead of God, but Judas Maccabeus and his brothers made a treaty with Rome, and the book that tells it approves. Jewish and Christian readers have weighed the two ever since.

sections.b: Isaiah pronounced woe on the envoys who went down to Egypt for help instead of asking the LORD (Isaiah 30:1–5; Isaiah 31:1–3). The prophet Hanani rebuked King Asa for paying the king of Aram: "Because you leaned on the king of Aram and did not lean on the LORD your God" (2 Chronicles 16:7). Hosea mocked Israel for running between Egypt and Assyria (Hosea 7:11). Behind these warnings stood Deuteronomy's ban on covenants with the nations of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:2) and the psalm's word: "Do not rely on nobles" (Psalm 146:3).
sections.refs: Isaiah 30:1–5; Isaiah 31:1–3; 2 Chronicles 16:7–9; Hosea 7:11; Deuteronomy 7:2; Psalm 146:3

sections.b: Other passages accept treaties with foreigners. Abraham made covenants with Abimelech and with Amorite allies (Genesis 14:13; Genesis 21:27). Solomon made a treaty with Hiram of Tyre (1 Kings 5:12). Joshua's oath to the Gibeonites, though won by a trick, was kept, and breaking it later brought famine (Joshua 9:15–19; 2 Samuel 21:1–2). The line most readers draw is between a treaty and trust: a treaty may be lawful, but relying on it in place of God is not.

1 Maccabees 8 tells of Judas's embassy to Rome and the treaty that followed, about 161 BC. Jonathan and Simon renewed it (1 Maccabees 12:1–4; 1 Maccabees 14:16–24; 1 Maccabees 15:15–24). The book praises Rome's loyalty to its friends without a word of warning. Josephus, writing after Rome had destroyed the Temple, retells the treaty (Antiquities 12.414–419). A saying in the Talmud says that Rome "kept faith with Israel twenty-six years" before it began to oppress it (Bavli Avodah Zarah 8b). Christian writers have pointed to the outcome, Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC, as a lesson in trusting a pagan power.
